extracted.intended_audience: clinicians and other healthcare professionals who act as peer reviewers for The BMJ
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for clinicians/researchers who review manuscripts for The BMJ, covering responsibilities, open (signed) peer review, declarations of competing interests, procedural steps, and where to find training and policy resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open (signed) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ uses open peer review: reviewers have to sign their reports, saying briefly who they are and where they work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must sign their reports and declare to the editors any competing interests that might relate to articles they have been asked to review. Open peer review does not mean authors should contact reviewers directly to discuss their reports; all queries must be directed through the editorial office. If reviewers experience any adverse event arising from open peer review, or wish to report views, they should email papersadmin@bmj.com.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should declare to the editors any competing interests that might relate to articles they have been asked to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations are made to the editors (as part of open peer review). See BMJ transparency policy for details on handling competing interests and related editorial policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary reviewer task: prioritise and assess for BMJ's aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to help prioritise manuscripts bearing in mind that The BMJ aims to publish original, important, and reliable articles that will help readers (mainly doctors) make better decisions about practice, policy, education, and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising a manuscript reviewers should focus on originality, importance, and reliability, and consider the article's likely usefulness to BMJ readers. All research in The BMJ is published with open access, which may influence assessment of audience and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive critiques to inform editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers advise the editors by providing constructive critiques that help editors assess a manuscript's importance and originality; editors are responsible for the final decision to accept or reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best reviews constructively critique the article and assist editors in judging importance and originality. The BMJ offers recognition (in partnership with the Cleveland Clinic Foundation) of up to 3 AMA PRA Category 1 CME points for such high-quality reviews. Reviewers should be aware that their reports may be used by editors to make transfer decisions within the BMJ family of journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural expectations: invitation response and review sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: If asked to review, reviewers will be emailed and must accept or reject the reviewing invitation via The BMJ's online editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts sent for review are usually seen by at least two reviewers. Reviewers can access each other's reports on the same manuscript once The BMJ has made its decision. Authors can nominate other BMJ journals to which their manuscript should be passed if rejected; editors' comments and peer reviewers' reports may be transferred to facilitate review at the next BMJ journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and communication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review requires signing reports but does not permit direct contact between authors and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All queries between authors and reviewers should be directed through the editorial office rather than direct contact. Reviewers should be mindful that their signed reports may later be seen by authors and by other editors within the BMJ Group if transferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use BMJ transparency policy for ethical concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should consult The BMJ transparency policy if they are concerned about ethics aspects of a manuscript or suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transparency policy consolidates editorial policies and provides advice on what to do if ethical issues arise during review. Reviewers should alert editors when they suspect ethical problems rather than handle these issues independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article provenance statement categories
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of every accepted editorial, research article, clinical review, practice article, analysis article, feature, and head-to-head article, The BMJ will add a statement explaining the article's provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provenance options listed by The BMJ are: 'Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed', 'Not commissioned; not externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned; externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned; not externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; externally peer reviewed', and 'Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; not externally peer reviewed.' Reviewers should be aware these provenance labels will appear on accepted articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review reuse and transfer within BMJ Group
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews and editors' comments may be passed to other BMJ journals if the author nominates transfer on submission or if the manuscript is rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The submission system can pass on editors' comments and peer reviewers' reports to facilitate review at the next BMJ Journal. Reviewers should therefore write reports with the understanding that their comments may be seen by other editors within the BMJ Group in future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, recognition and feedback for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ provides resources for reviewers including 'Becoming a BMJ reviewer', peer review training materials, and detailed guidance; they welcome feedback from reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BMJ offers training materials and an ongoing programme of editorial research (including randomised controlled trials on open peer review and peer review training). Reviewers who produce the best, constructive critiques may receive CME credit. Reviewers are invited to provide feedback on manuscripts reviewed and on the review process in general.
